evidence: Draft judged: 'Is this way of responding helping you to be clearer and steadier and less hooked?' In CONTEXT.txt it appears once, as the closing sentence of the section 'A response check, not a verdict about what it is', right after 'You don't have to find out if it's a guard immediately, and you may not be able to comfort it quickly.' Read cold, it follows: you need not know what it is, so here is what to ask instead, and it is the check the heading promises. The contrast with identity ('not a verdict about what it is') is carried by the heading and that sentence, so dropping the frame 'The useful question is' loses no claim. Pronouns (C02): through the section 'it' means the thing that comes up, and the draft avoids 'it' and uses his 'this way of responding' instead, which echoes the heading's 'response check' and points at the response the reader is already taking (warm or arm's length, the Nurturer, stopping). 'this' has no single named antecedent, but the heading and the paragraphs before anchor it; the swap also removes the clash an 'it' meaning the response would have had with the 'it' of the thing. Against SOURCE.txt ('The useful question is whether this way of responding helps you become clearer, steadier, and less hooked.') the meaning is kept: the same test with the same three outcomes in his order, now asked directly. Shifts I checked, none adding a fact: 'helps you become' to 'is helping you to be' (asks about now, which suits an in-the-moment check), the frame dropped, and commas to 'and ... and' (see O14). Nothing about Joel's life or any study is added (C03 and C04 absent). Linter findings. D9 follows the source order: one sentence replaced by one question, so order is trivial, and the section around it keeps its own asides and concessions ('If, however', 'if that feels okay', 'you may not be able to comfort it quickly'), so T13 and T09 do not apply. E36/E41 heavy second person: 6.7 per 100 words, the section is addressed to 'you' throughout, and the draft has one 'you', as the sentence it replaces did. O14 repeated 'and': the shape is exactly 'X and Y and Z', the device Joel's 2026-10-07 note calls Emulate's trick in a list. I accept it here because it is a three-outcome check asked as a second-person question, which is speech register; the label itself calls that fine, and its own example, 'bread and butter and jam', has the same shape. The three terms are his published ones, so the 'and's add no item, the section already uses a repeated conjunction in a series ('sadness or fear or like you're trying to protect something'), and it occurs once. Residual risk for the writer to know: if the 2026-10-07 ruling was meant to cover any written three-item series, this one falls inside it; I read 'fine in speech' as covering a question to the reader like this. Other rows I looked at and found ABSENT: T02 (the section's step-by-step cadence predates the change, and the draft replaces the sentence that framed the check with the check itself), T12 (the triad is his published three), T15 (the structure changed from statement to question, so this is not word-swapping), T19, T20 (a closing check, no antithesis or quote-card turn), T21 (three outcomes of one question, not three argumentative jobs), T22 (it carries his stance: judge a response by its effect, not by naming the thing), T24 (the question is left for the reader, not answered), T26 ('response' and 'responding' echo the heading on purpose), T28 and T29 (the section stops at its check, with no uplift or restatement), C01. Note: the writer's ADMISSION.json reason for D9 lists asides ('if I can put it that way', 'of course', '!') that are not in this draft, so I judged D9 on its own merits.
